source.title: Self-Adaptive Training: beyond Empirical Risk Minimization
source.authors: Lang Huang; Chao Zhang; Hongyang Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains standard ERM models with stochastic gradient methods on CIFAR10 datasets with randomized labels and unstructured image corruptions, and reports training and generalization outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study's own ERM results on partially corrupted CIFAR10 training data bear on the claim. Results for self-adaptive training are not rows unless they directly measure the claimed behavior. Cited findings from other papers are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own ERM training accuracy and learning dynamics on randomly corrupted CIFAR10 data, using the same corruption schemes and behavioral measures as the original experiments. Its evidence concerns partial corruption rather than fully randomized datasets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: ERM memorizes corrupted training data after initially learning useful signal, whereas self-adaptive training mitigates overfitting and improves generalization across the studied corruptions. The authors also report benefits for noisy-label classification and selective classification.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ERM with ResNet-34 on CIFAR10 and partially corrupted training data, rather than the exact models and settings of the original studies; also evaluates Gaussian and pixel-shuffling corruptions.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise scheme and noise rate affect generalization error; removing data augmentation raises errors. ERM accuracy dynamics differ between untouched and corrupted examples over training.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing augmentation increases generalization gaps and clean-validation errors for ERM and self-adaptive training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation improves generalization under partial training-data corruption.

record.problems: Most relevant curves are figure-only, without exact values or uncertainty. The paper evaluates partial corruption rather than fully random labels and does not establish chance test error for the all-random-label setting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results omitted. Results for the self-adaptive method, unrelated applications, and cited prior work were not entered as rows.

untested.parts: Completely randomized training labels, chance test error in that setting, and a documented unchanged-hyperparameter comparison with true-label training.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions.
Zero training error on datasets consisting entirely of each unstructured-input type.
The full joint trajectory of perfect training fit and steadily rising test error through 100% label randomization, including the chance endpoint.
Weight-decay and dropout ablations; augmentation's inability to prevent fitting completely random labels; and whether removing regularization alone leaves true-label generalization good.
Learning dynamics with entirely random labels and direct measurements of learned shared representations.

missing.what: Figure 7 repeats the four corruption experiments at 80% corruption, and its caption says the Section 2 observations continue to hold. Add separate ERM fitting rows for each corruption type; exact terminal accuracies are unavailable in the supplied text.
missing.locator: Figure 7; Appendix B.2, Study on extreme noise

record.verdict_notes: Missing coverage of full randomization is untested scope, not evidence against the claims. The supplied figure text contains axes and legends but does not permit reliable numerical reconstruction of curves. Self-adaptive training changes the training targets and objective, so its reduced noisy-label fitting does not challenge claims about standard ERM.

versions.untested_parts: Tests partial random label corruption, not a dataset whose entire training set has random labels; test error at chance and unchanged hyperparameters relative to a true-label run are not established.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or convergence slowdown by corruption fraction.
Corrupts only a fraction of the CIFAR10 training set; does not report fitting a dataset made entirely of shuffled or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Reports trends in generalization error across noise rates and training accuracy under 40% corruption; does not establish that test error rises steadily all the way to chance while training accuracy remains perfect at every rate.
Appendix B.2 compares outcomes with and without data augmentation, but does not report whether augmentation prevents fitting random labels. Weight decay and dropout are not ablated for this claim.
Reports ERM accuracy on clean and corrupted portions over training, but does not measure feature or pattern representations directly.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: ERM training on CIFAR10 with 40% of training data corrupted by uniformly random labels.
rows.note: The paper states that ERM easily overfits the noisy training data and achieves nearly perfect training accuracy.
rows.check: Near-perfect fitting is explicitly reported at 40% label randomization. Common cropping and flipping augmentation were enabled, so this also bears on augmentation not preventing memorization. It does not establish fitting fully random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Measured ERM generalization error across random noise rates on CIFAR10 for four corruption schemes.

conditions.value: corrupted labels, Gaussian, random pixels, shuffled pixels

rows.note: The authors state that ERM generalization errors consistently grow as injected noise increases. This is generalization error, not a numeric test-error series.
rows.check: The measure is the noisy-training versus noisy-validation accuracy gap, not test error. Its increase cannot independently establish increasing test error with perfect training fit at every noise rate. Split label corruption from the three input-corruption schemes; only label corruption directly bears on V4.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Measured ERM accuracy against correct labels on untouched and randomized portions of CIFAR10 training data over training epochs.
rows.measure: Training accuracy on each portion over epochs
rows.value: Figure only; text says ERM fits correct labels in the first few epochs and eventually overfits the corrupted labels.
rows.note: The figure's accuracy values are not supplied in the text; the stated trend is explicit.
rows.check: The substantive trend is correct. The discussion is Appendix B.2, with Figure 8 appearing near Appendix A.2. The text additionally states that correct-label accuracy on the corrupted portion eventually falls to zero; this is not zero accuracy against assigned noisy labels.

source_check.correct: Discussion: Appendix B.2; Figure 8. Correct-label accuracy on the corrupted portion initially increases, then eventually decreases to 0.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 8 caption, page 14; Appendix B.2, page 15
source_check.problem: The discussion locator is Appendix B.2, rather than Appendix A.2; the reported result is correct.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Compared ERM and self-adaptive training with data augmentation turned off on CIFAR10 with random noise.

conditions.value: four random noise schemes; noise-rate sweep

rows.measure: Generalization error and clean validation error
rows.baseline: ERM with common data augmentation in the earlier experiments
rows.value: Figure only; authors report that errors rise without augmentation for both ERM and their method
rows.note: This comparison concerns generalization under noise, not whether augmentation prevents fitting random labels.
rows.check: Higher generalization gaps and validation errors without augmentation do not establish whether augmentation prevents random-label fitting, or whether removing it makes true-label generalization poor. Separate ERM from self-adaptive training rather than combining subjects.
